title: ‘Self-styled Chanakya’ Amit Shah fails to muster majority for delimitation: Congress
description: Jairam Ramesh Says Mallikarjun Kharge Has Written To PM Modi Four Times Seeking Talks On The Bills And Is Still Awaiting An Acknowledgement
author: PTI
content:
The Congress on Wednesday said party president Mallikarjun Kharge had written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi four times to propose talks on delimitation, but had yet to receive an acknowledgement. It accused the government of using inducements, pressure and division in an unsuccessful bid to secure a two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha for the bills.
Congress general secretary in charge of communications Jairam Ramesh invoked Kautilya’s four-fold doctrine of ‘saam, daam, dand, bhed’ from the Arthashastra. ‘Saam’ means dialogue, ‘daam’ refers to financial inducements, ‘dand’ to punishment or institutional pressure, and ‘bhed’ to creating division.
“In his desperate search for a super-tainted two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha to get the diabolical delimitation bills passed, the self-styled Chanakya has been resorting to the last three and has failed,” Ramesh said, asking why the government had given dialogue no chance.
“The Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge ji has written suggesting this precise route to the PM four times in the past seven months - April 11, July 16, Aug 27 and Oct 16 - but there has not even been a routine acknowledgement to these letters,” he said.
Ramesh often refers to Union home minister Amit Shah as the “self-styled Chanakya”.
The Congress had said on Monday that the continued uncertainty over the Parliament session suggested the “PM-HM jodi” was being trapped by its own bluff and bluster or that something “truly sinister” was in the works.
The party alleged that either way, the “two GTA (Gyanesh Theft Arrangers)” stars stood brutally exposed and that the actions of the “diabolical duo” were diminishing Parliament as an institution.
Last week, the Congress said 100 days had passed since Parliament’s monsoon session was adjourned sine die and that Modi and Shah were still seeking a “supertainted” two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha to pass the delimitation bill.
Ramesh had said it was in the national interest to retain the Lok Sabha’s current strength and state-wise seat allocation, with one-third reservation for women in place until the Viksit Bharat objective was achieved.

title: NSA Ajit Doval calls for stronger regional security cooperation to tackle Indian Ocean threats
description: The National Security Advisor Highlights The Role Of The Colombo Security Conclave In Advancing India's Neighbourhood First Outlook And MAHASAGAR Vision
author: PTI
content:
National Security Advisor Ajit Doval on Wednesday called for deeper strategic cooperation among Indian Ocean nations to address evolving security challenges, reaffirming India's commitment to strengthening collective regional security.
Addressing the eighth Colombo Security Conclave (CSC) in Male, Doval highlighted several pressing security challenges facing the region and stressed the need for closer cooperation among member countries to enhance their collective capabilities.
"The Colombo Security Conclave represents the intersection of our Neighborhood First outlook and the MAHASAGAR vision," Doval said.
"We are committed to continue working closely with the CSC countries to enhance our collective capacities in dealing with the evolving serious security challenges," he added.
Doval expressed confidence that the CSC would emerge as an effective regional instrument to ensure collective security and safeguard common interests in the Indian Ocean.
"India has been trying to work very closely with Sri Lanka, with the Maldives and other countries, and we want to see that this cooperation is further extended," the NSA said.
"I assure all of you that India, as one of the countries which had initiated the idea of the Colombo Security Conclave, will give its best and will try to give all necessary help, assistance. I assure you of our fullest commitment to achieve our common objectives," Doval added.
The CSC has emerged as a key regional security grouping of Indian Ocean littoral states, comprising India, Sri Lanka, the Maldives, Mauritius, Bangladesh and Seychelles. Its focus areas include maritime safety, counter-terrorism and transnational security cooperation.
The grouping was established in 2020 after India, Sri Lanka and the Maldives agreed to expand the scope and membership of their trilateral meeting on maritime cooperation.
Its cooperation framework rests on five pillars: maritime safety and security; countering terrorism and radicalisation; combating trafficking and transnational organised crime; cyber security and protection of critical infrastructure; and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief.
Doval's remarks come in the context of India's MAHASAGAR vision, which Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced during his visit to Mauritius last March. MAHASAGAR stands for 'Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions' and outlines India's engagement with the Global South.

title: Inflation: How rising food prices are squeezing Indian households
description: India's food inflation is broadening, squeezing household budgets.
author: Soutik Biswas
content:
The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
- Published
India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data, external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.
With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, external, India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
A survey by polling agency LocalCircles found that six in 10 consumers say household essentials cost them over 20% more each month than a year ago, prompting calls for government intervention.
Rising prices are also forcing cutbacks: 74% are curbing discretionary spending on eating out, shopping and entertainment, while half are buying smaller quantities of essentials.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.
"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
The numbers bear this out.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.
In urban India, the corresponding rates were 6.1% and 5.3%.
The pressure is visible even in the cost of a simple meal.
Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis, external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.
Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.
And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.
Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.
The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives.
Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.
Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer.
"The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.
Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.
Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later.
Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to Sharma
There are other pressures.
Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.
To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.
Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks, external are particularly ample.
There is a wider economic risk, says Sengupta.
"Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.
For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.
Agriculture is a relatively low-productivity sector, and the government has long sought to protect farmers by setting minimum support prices (MSPs) for certain crops - a price floor at which it promises to buy produce, helping farmers guard against a market crash.
At the same time, food prices are politically sensitive. Sharp increases in the price of staples such as onions and tomatoes can quickly anger consumers, prompting governments to step in with measures such as restricting exports, limiting how much traders can stockpile, or otherwise trying to bring prices down.
The broader story of India's changing food consumption makes the current inflation more interesting.
Households are eating differently from a decade ago. An analysis, external of the 2011-12 and 2023-24 consumption surveys shows that the share of cereals in food spending has fallen sharply, particularly among the poorest households, reflecting the impact of subsidised food programmes.
Meanwhile, consumption of nutrient-rich foods such as dairy, fruit and meat has increased across income groups, with the biggest gains among the poorest, the study revealed.
India's food basket is becoming more diverse. But diversity is meaningful only if ordinary Indians can afford it. Ultimately, food inflation is about what makes it to the plate - and what has to be left out.

title: US preparing to unveil plan for new tariffs on global trading partners
description: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.
author: Jonathan Josephs, Osmond Chia
content:
US preparing to unveil plan for new tariffs on global trading partners
- Published
The US is preparing to announce plans for new tariffs on several countries as early as Wednesday, the BBC understands.
The new import taxes would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union and Japan among at least 14 jurisdictions affected.
The move comes after the White House's so-called "Section 301" investigation. It was launched in March after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.
Trump has made tariffs a signature policy of his presidency, arguing that they will help boost American manufacturing and create jobs.
The president sent shockwaves around the world when he unveiled sweeping tariffs on global trading partners in April 2025 shortly after his return to the White House.
While the tariffs were later struck down, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued then that overproduction abroad was displacing American manufacturing and deterring investment.
Under the new tariffs, countries will face different import tax rates depending on the deals that they have previously struck with Trump.
The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, which remain locked in a trade dispute.
Despite last week's meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping, the two sides have yet to fully resolve their difference with an interim agreement set to expire on 10 January.
In the run up to the Shenzhen summit, the US accused China of not fully living up to the terms of what it agreed in October 2025.
Washington said Beijing was falling short on its commitments, "particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals".
However earlier on Tuesday China extended the suspension of a ban on exports critical minerals including gallium, germanium, antimony until 27 January. The ban would otherwise have come into force on Friday.
The Trump administration's tariff policy has been criticised for putting up prices for American consumers and damaging the global economy.
  - Published22 August

title: Bangladesh's ex-PM Sheikh Hasina says she plans to return on 16 December
description: Hasina has spoken several times of her desire to return, but this is the first time she has set a date.
author: Zoya Mateen
content:
Bangladesh's ex-PM Sheikh Hasina says she plans to return on 16 December
- Published
Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she plans to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power.
Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson said.
The announcement comes amid renewed unrest in Bangladesh, where supporters of her Awami League party have staged protests despite a ban on its activities.
But it's unclear how Hasina will return. Last year, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on student-led protests that ended her 15-year rule. She denies the charges.
Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir dismissed the prospect of Hasina returning on her own terms.
"Sheikh Hasina will not be able to return to the country as an ordinary commercial passenger; she will be brought back in handcuffs," he told a press briefing on Tuesday.
Kabir also accused Hasina and Delhi of fomenting recent unrest in Bangladesh, alleging that they were backing "terrorist activities" in the country.
India's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In April, the ministry said it was examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties".
Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as tens of thousands of protesters descended on Dhaka, and crowds stormed her official residence.
What began as student protests against quotas in government jobs turned into a mass uprising against her government following a deadly crackdown on demonstrators. The UN estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.
On Tuesday, Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali accused Bangladeshi authorities of forcing her into exile in violation of the country's constitution.
"Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on 5 August 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," he said in a statement.
The choice of date is significant. Bangladesh celebrates Victory Day on 16 December, marking the end of its 1971 war of independence from Pakistan. Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led the country's independence movement.
Abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, described her decision as "deeply symbolic". "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people," he said, expressing confidence that she would once again lead Bangladesh.
Hasina's announcement - and Dhaka's sharp response to it - come at a time when the ousted leader is seeking to reassert her political relevance from exile.
The Awami League was banned from political activities in May last year under the interim government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus, which took charge after Hasina's ouster.
The party was subsequently barred from contesting February's general election, which brought its long-time rival, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), to power, with Tarique Rahman becoming prime minister.
But the ban has not put an end to street protests by Awami League supporters, who have also called for nationwide shutdowns demanding Hasina's return.
Hasina, meanwhile, has repeatedly spoken of her desire to return to Bangladesh, even as she has acknowledged the risks of doing so.
"I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she told a gathering of journalists in Delhi over an audio link in August, on the second anniversary of her ouster.
Hasina's continued political activities from Indian soil have also complicated Delhi's efforts to rebuild ties with Dhaka.
India enjoyed close relations with Hasina during her 15 years in power and had hoped that the election of a new government in Bangladesh would offer an opportunity to reset ties, which deteriorated sharply after her ouster.
But nine months after taking office, Rahman is yet to visit India despite an invitation. He has travelled to China, Japan and Malaysia, and skipped the BRICS summit hosted by India in September.
Discussions over a possible visit in August coincided with anger in Dhaka over Hasina's remarks to journalists in Delhi.
The two countries have since resumed talks about a visit, but no dates have been announced.

title: Prohibitory orders, detentions as Vijay govt defies SC order. Karthigai Deepam not lit at Deepathoon
description: Vijay govt's decision triggered protests by Hindu activists, leading to scuffles with police near the Thiruparankundram temple, while BJP leaders were detained.
author: Shweta Tripathi
content:
Chennai: The Vijay-led TVK government Tuesday defied the Supreme Court order permitting a one-time lighting of the Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon, as the ceremonial lamp was lit at the traditional location near the Uchi Pillayar Temple atop the Thiruparankundram hill in Tamil Nadu’s Madurai.
No lamp was lit on the disputed stone pillar even after the Madras High Court directed the Madurai district administration to comply with the Supreme Court’s orders.
Expressing the TVK’s clear stance, Law Minister CTR Nirmal Kumar wrote on X, “The Karthigai Mahadeepam was lit in the Deepa Mandapam near the Uchchipillaiyar temple located directly above the head of the presiding deity at Thiruparankundram.”
The decision triggered protests by Hindu activists and members of organisations including the Hindu Munnani, leading to scuffles with police near the Thiruparankundram temple. Nearly 50 protesters were detained after a confrontation in which two policemen sustained minor injuries.
BJP leader Tamilisai Soundararajan criticised Kumar. “A law minister gleefully posts about violating the Supreme Court’s order. Who is the message you are posting now meant for? As law minister, opposing the Supreme Court’s interim action is condemnable. The Tamil Nadu law minister is losing the moral right to remain in office. This government must answer for its conduct in disregarding Hindu sentiments and the law…” she wrote on X.
The Madras High Court’s Madurai bench had earlier directed the district administration to comply with the Supreme Court’s 20 November ruling. That order—passed by a bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M. Pancholi—had stayed key findings of the High Court’s January judgment that treated the lighting of the ceremonial lamp at the Deepathoon as an essential religious practice.
The apex court permitted a strictly limited, one-time lighting on Tuesday, the day of the Karthigai Deepam festival, by a small authorised team from the temple Devasthanam and government officials. Public access, processions and demonstrations were barred, and the court made it clear that the permission created no customary, religious or proprietary right and would not serve as a precedent.
The Tamil Nadu government filed a review petition specifically challenging the one-time permission portion of the 20 November order, arguing it contains an error apparent on the face of the record. In its petition in SC earlier to stay the Madras High Court order to allow lighting of the lamp at the Deepathoon, the State had cited historical records, including a 1996 High Court order confirming the traditional location, and argued that the HC had effectively sought to create a new practice through a writ petition.
Both the Vijay-led TVK government as well as the DMK before it have opposed the lighting of the lamp at the Deepathoon—which is located close to a dargah—arguing that it is not an established temple custom, that the ritual has been performed at the Deepa Mandapam for over 150 years, and that altering the long-standing practice risks law and order.
On Tuesday, the TVK’s alliance partner VCK lauded its decision. VCK chief Thirumavalavan congratulated the government and appreciated the district collector and officials of the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department for lighting the grand lamp at the Deepa Mandapam near the Ucchi Pillayar Temple, as is customary. He also thanked CM Vijay for “thwarting the Sangh Parivar’s conspiracy and safeguarding social harmony in Tamil Nadu”, he wrote on X.
Prohibitory orders, detentions
The Madurai District Collector imposed prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS, banning assemblies, agitations, processions, public meetings and any unauthorised climbing of the hill until 10 am on Wednesday. Over 5,600 police personnel were deployed, the area was declared a temporary Red Zone with a drone ban, and the Deepathoon was barricaded.
Tamil Nadu BJP president Nainar Nagenthran was detained while heading towards Madurai from Tirunelveli. Former Union Minister L. Murugan was stopped in Coimbatore district and placed under house arrest. The BJP alleged that around 750 of its leaders and Hindu Munnani functionaries across southern districts were confined or prevented from travelling. Hindu Munnani members were also arrested in other places while attempting to proceed to the hill with ritual items.
The Madras High Court later directed the release of those unlawfully detained under the prohibitory orders.
(Edited by Gitanjali Das)
Also Read: CM Vijay’s popularity is intact, but his government in Tamil Nadu is facing a political storm

title: 120 seats sought, 26 seats offered: Why Congress-SP alliance talks for UP polls hit roadblock in Round 2
description: The Congress currently has two MLAs in the 403-member Uttar Pradesh Assembly, while the SP has 111. UP goes to polls next year.
author: Prashant Srivastava
content:
Lucknow: Seat-sharing talks between the Samajwadi Party (SP) and Congress for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections have hit a roadblock. While the Congress has sought 120 seats, the SP has offered only 26 in its initial proposal.
For the second round of talks Tuesday, SP leaders arrived with a list of 26 seats, which did not go down well with the Congress leaders in attendance. According to sources in the know, the Congress instead sought discussions on all 403 assembly constituencies, arguing that seat-sharing should be decided on the basis of political and electoral calculations.
Tuesday’s talks come a day after the first round that lasted all of 20 minutes. Both parties’ representatives had met at the Delhi residence of senior Congress leader and Rajya Sabha MP Pramod Tiwari. During the meeting, the Congress submitted a list of 120 constituencies where it wants to contest. In response, the SP shared its preferred list of 26 seats for the Congress Tuesday.
ThePrint has learnt that the SP leaders indicated that the number could be increased after consultations with the party’s central leadership, but made it clear that the final offer was unlikely to cross 50 seats. This did not go down well with the Congress representatives present at the meeting.
SP Rajya Sabha MP Ram Gopal Yadav, it is learnt, defended his party’s proposal, citing the Congress’s electoral performance in the 2022 assembly elections. “Two of these seats were won by the Congress, and it finished second in four others. The remaining 20 seats are those where we received 60,000 to 70,000 votes, while the Congress got only around 2,000 votes,” he is learnt to have said.
जीतनेवाली पहली ‘26 सीटों’ से हुई है शुरुआत
मिलजुलकर समझदारी से और आगे बढ़ेगी बात
— Akhilesh Yadav (@yadavakhilesh) November 24, 2026
The Congress currently has just two MLAs in Uttar Pradesh and secured less than three percent of the votes in the 2022 assembly elections. The SP won 111 seats in 2022, securing 32.06 percent of the total vote share.
Asked whether a final agreement could be reached soon, Yadav said seats would be allocated on the basis of the Congress’s strength and that constituencies where it had performed poorly would be difficult to offer.
A Congress leader who was present at the meeting, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the SP’s offer was far below the party’s expectations. “Until yesterday, the SP was calling our demand impractical. Now, its own offer is extremely modest. An alliance cannot work with just 26 or 40 seats. Uttar Pradesh has 80 Lok Sabha constituencies. Even if we get one assembly seat in each Lok Sabha constituency, that would mean 80 seats. Our demand is for 100 seats. The SP can remove 20 constituencies from our original list of 120, but it should offer us at least 100.”
The leader added that the Congress would place the SP’s proposal before its central leadership, which was also unlikely to accept it. The final decision on how to proceed would now rest with the party high command.
How SP arrived at its 26-seat proposal
According to a senior SP functionary, the party has divided the proposed 26 constituencies into three categories, primarily on the basis of the Congress’s performance in the 2022 assembly elections.
The list includes the two seats won by the Congress in 2022—Rampur Khas and Pharenda—and four constituencies where it finished second—Mathura, Kheragarh, Jagdishpur and Kidwai Nagar.
The remaining 20 seats are spread across different regions. In western Uttar Pradesh and the Braj region, these include Baghpat, Modinagar, Hapur, Jewar, Siyana, Khurja, Khair, Iglas, Mant, Agra North and Fatehpur Sikri. In Awadh and central Uttar Pradesh, the proposed seats are Bilgram-Mallanwan, Govind Nagar and Nanpara. In eastern UP, the list includes Gorakhpur City, Khajani, Padrauna, Fazilnagar, Pindra and Varanasi Cantt. Interestingly, only one seat from the Rae Bareli and Amethi districts is on the SP’s list.
Sources said the SP has also asked the Congress to share the names of its potential candidates, along with details of caste equations and electoral calculations, for constituencies beyond the 26 seats proposed by the party.
After the meeting, Ram Gopal Yadav described the discussions as positive. Responding to questions about the short duration of the meeting, he said complicated issues take time to resolve but expressed hope that an agreement would be reached within the next two to three days.
SP MP Rajeev Rai also said both parties were examining constituencies individually and that the candidates’ winnability would be the only criterion for ticket distribution.
2024 versus 2022
According to sources, the Congress is basing its demand for a larger share of seats on its performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, when it contested 17 constituencies in alliance with the SP and won six. The party secured a vote share of 9.46 percent.
The Congress believes it can bring Dalit, Brahmin and Extremely Backward Caste voters into the alliance’s fold. It also wants representation in almost every district to strengthen its organisational presence ahead of the assembly elections.
The SP, however, is relying on the Congress’s assembly election record. In 2022, the Congress contested 399 seats independently but managed to win only two, securing a vote share of 2.33 percent. Its candidates forfeited their deposits in 387 constituencies.
Even in the 2017 assembly elections, when the Congress contested in alliance with the SP, it won only seven of the 114 seats it contested.
The SP’s argument is that the Congress’s improved performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections was a result of the combined strength of the alliance and should not be treated as an indication of its independent electoral strength.
Congress has also sought 8 out of 10 assembly constituencies in Amethi and Rae Bareli districts. However, in the 2022 assembly elections, the SP won six of these seats, while the BJP secured the remaining four. The Congress failed to win even one seat in the two districts.
The party, however, believes that changing political equations, including cross-voting by some SP MLAs during the 2024 Rajya Sabha elections, could give it room to stake a claim in these constituencies.
(Edited by Gitanjali Das)

title: 8 km for Rs 50 bottle: Manipur’s ethnic strife hit old liquor supply routes, then a deadly trade took over
description: In Manipur's Chakpikarong, men once travelled to Sugnu for an evening drink. Now, children have lost fathers, families are demanding accountability after 16 died of suspected spurious liquor.
author: Samridhi Tewari
content:
Chandel, Manipur: An 8-kilometre journey, a Rs 50 jeep ride from Chakpikarong to Sugnu to buy a Rs 50 plastic bottle of country-made liquor—this was the routine followed for decades by many residents of a quiet village of the Anal tribe in Manipur’s Chakpikarong area of Chandel district.
But a lot has changed since last week. Sixteen villagers died after drinking the liquor, and the others fear the liquor is poisoned.
While there have been reports of people falling ill in other districts of Manipur too after drinking the spurious liquor, including Imphal and Kakching, Chandel recorded that most deaths—16 of the 17 in the state.
The government continues its crackdown on vendors and suppliers to ensure a complete ban on the sale of country-made liquor.
Manipur Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh Monday met representatives of various Anal tribal civil society organisations to discuss the suspected spurious liquor tragedy. The representatives submitted a memorandum seeking immediate intervention by the state government, the Chief Minister’s Office CMO said.
What has unfolded in Chakpikarong is more than a suspected spurious liquor tragedy. It has exposed a shadowy network of country-made liquor moving across district boundaries, the breakdown of older supply routes following the 2023 ethnic violence, and the absence of effective regulation in a state where prohibition has long shaped drinking habits.
Six people have been arrested so far, while several others have been detained in connection with the spurious liquor deaths. As police began mapping the supply chain, they zeroed in on Andro village, from where suppliers bought the liquor and sold it in the Sugnu area.
Families are now demanding answers about who made the spurious liquor, who sold it and why it reached their villages unchecked.
Died in the middle of the night
Nungpan is a quiet, green village. Only a few houses dot the neighbourhood, and most residents are from the Anal tribe.
B. Beruwng, born in 1973, had lived a comfortable life here with his three brothers, their wives, and his dogs, cats and chickens. He would work on his farm all day, and in the evening, take a jeep to Sugnu, buy three bottles of liquor, drink one and carry the others back home.
Beruwng followed the same routine on 17 November. After returning from Sugnu in the evening, he went to sleep alone in his room. And then everything changed.
“We were all sleeping, when he heard him scream. He said his stomach was exploding, we assumed he was having stomach pain, so we gave him water. He couldn’t breathe, or see, but as it was late at night, we couldn’t take him to the hospital,” Beruwng’s brother, Joseph Anal, told ThePrint.
“My brother was a simple man. He wanted his liquor at night. Here in our village, most people are from Anal tribe, and generally do not consume liquor,” he said. Which is why, people bought their liquor from basements and homes in Sugnu.
The next morning, on 18 November, when the family went into Beruwng’s room, he was dead. “My brother didn’t even get to speak his last words, or explain what happened,” Joseph said.
Soon, news of the spurious liquor tragedy spread across the village, and more people reported similar symptoms. “There were people complaining of their stomach almost exploding, vomiting blood, not being able to see, their bodies were burning. That is when we were able to understand what had happened,” Joseph told ThePrint.
Joseph says people in his village have stopped drinking. “People are scared. What if all liquor bottles have that poison?”
A decades-old culture comes to a pause
Kishun Hrangbung, 40, from the Naga community, cultivated plants for a living in Nungpan village in Manipur. He too drank liquor in Sugnu before returning home. He started vomiting when he reached home and struggled through the night.
In the morning, he was taken to the Community Health Centre Chakpikarong, but he died within 30 minutes, his brother said.
As the family mourns Kishun’s death, their anger is palpable. “We demand answers,” they say. “Kishun, and so many other men who have died in our village, made a mistake by consuming alcohol. But, the government has to take strong action against the perpetrators. Who was responsible for making this spurious liquor? Who was responsible for selling it, and then distributing it to our people? Who will take responsibility?”
His uncle has kept the two bottles Kishun brought from Sugnu. “I don’t know what to do with these two bottles that killed him. Am I to throw them away? Will the police need it? It haunts us every single day… knowing it was a bottle of alcohol that killed him,” Hrangbung Bebising, Kishun’s uncle told ThePrint.
The first bottle, made of plastic and resembling a regular water bottle, bears the name ‘Andro’, with ‘packaged drinking wine’ written below it. The second says ‘Nagola Pamjaba’, with ‘premium quality’ written below the logo. The bottle claims the contents are ‘brewed from the finest rice grains of Manipur’.
Bebising understands that there are no licenced liquor shops in the area, but he has a question: “Why is liquor being sold with no licence then? Shouldn’t the government do something about it? You can’t ban liquor, but can you not enforce stronger regulations?”
Nungpan is a Christian village with its own strict rules. Residents say the sale of liquor is prohibited. So, anyone who wants to drink has to go to Sugnu to procure it.
The ethnic violence also changed the way liquor was supplied to the village. Bebising explains that earlier, members of the Zou community in Sugnu used to make alcohol. They would share the liquor they made and even allow people to sit in their homes and drink. Public transport was available back then, and buses also plied on the route. A few Meiteis made liquor as well.
“After 2023, the Zou community had to flee the area to Churachandpur. Now, people have to get the smuggled liquor from Sungu. They go on two-wheelers, or four-wheelers,” he said.
Rice and sugar as compensation for deaths
Almost everyone in Manipur’s Chakpikarong is a farmer. They work on their own plots of land during the day, as do their children.
P. Moruwng, 57, did the same. A resident of Toupokpi village, he had three sons, who had also begun working with him. His wife had died 15 years ago.
“He, too, began experiencing similar symptoms after he returned from Sugnu on Friday evening. His stomach was burning, and was vomiting blood, so we told him that we’ll take him to the Community Health Centre. Since it’s a village, it takes time to find a vehicle; when we finally did find a vehicle after 20 minutes, we went to his room, and asked him to stand. He couldn’t. Papa was no more,” his son, Sumpi Moning Anal told ThePrint.
In Toupokpi village, most children do not go to college. They attend government schools but often drop out later. The violence that broke out in Manipur in 2023 made it even more difficult for students to travel to different parts of the state.
Moruwng sons are 25, 23 and 13 years old. They are not sure what will happen next. But they say the local government helped them with compensation.
“We were given daal, rice, and sugar as compensation. We were told if we require more, we can request. I don’t know about jobs… what job will I get? What am I supposed to do after my papa’s death?”
(Edited by Viny Mishra)

title: Fact-Check: Viral Video of a Raccoon Protecting Her Babies Is AI-Generated
description: Fact-Check: An AI-generated video is going viral on social media with false claims that it shows a raccoon refusing to leave a flooded car until all her babies are safe and out of danger.
author: Anika K
content:
A video is going viral on social media, claiming to show a raccoon refusing to leave a flooded car until all her babies were safe and out of danger.
- News organisation News9 were among the accounts sharing the video.
How did we find out?: We ran a reverse image search on the video using Google Lens and found a Facebook reel with the same visuals.
- The video is captioned, "Rescue crews battling the Kentucky flood found a mother raccoon on the roof of a sinking car, refusing to leave her three babies… what she did next left the whole crew in tears. Would you have risked it?
- However, the video has an AI tag, added by the user.
- We went through the Facebook page and found out that they have posted several similar AI-generated videos.
- The account bio reads, "Generated videos for fun, surprise and good vibes."
Is the video AI?: We ran the video through Hive Moderation, an AI detector, which flagged it as 98.3 percent likely to have been AI-generated.
- We also ran the video through DeepFake-O-Meter, and three of its detectors flagged the viral clip as AI-generated.
Conclusion: The video is AI-generated and doesn't show real footage of a raccoon protecting her babies.
(Not convinced of a post or information you came across online and want it verified? Send us the details on WhatsApp at 9540511818 , or e-mail it to us at webqoof@thequint.com and we'll fact-check it for you. You can also read all our fact-checked stories here.)

title: Inside Phey, Ladakh, Where Water Lords and Household Rotas Govern Shared Resources
description: At 3,180–3,186 metres, Phey shares scarce meltwater through household turns. A stone check, a water lord and livestock rules reveal Ladakh’s village governance.
author: Avantika Krishna
content:
Before dawn, a farmer in Phey may be waiting for a turn that belongs to a carefully watched village schedule. Water is not taken whenever someone needs it. Its flow is shared through rules, turns, and people tasked with ensuring nobody takes more than their share.
At 3,180 – 3,186 metres in Ladakh’s cold desert, this is how the community manages scarce resources through duties.
A water turn is a village responsibility
Phey lies west of Leh town. Its irrigation story begins beyond its fields. The village shares a stream with upstream Phyang. Winter snowfall and spring weather influence when meltwater arrives and how much reaches the channels. Springs also feed ponds that supply some fields, while upper fields rely more heavily on the stream arriving from Phyang. The water’s arrival is tied to the thaw, so a poor winter or cool spring can affect sowing and irrigation.
A study by Dorjey Angchok, Tsering Stobdan and Shashi B Singh, using 1981 village-directory data, gives Phey 33 households and 176 people. It records household-based water distribution, rather than a channel-based rota, because the settlement was relatively small. These are historical figures, not a current population count.
The chhur-pon, literally the “water lord”, coordinates irrigation. The supervisor knows which field gets water, when and in what order. In Phey, the role works alongside a rota for guarding the main water-control point.
Households take turns sending people to watch the main sluice, or yur-go, that controls the main channel. Two people from each household are selected in rotation to check for blockages, overflow, or damage. When water is scarce, some must keep watch at night.
The village devised a way to verify that guards reached the control point. Each person breaks a stone in two, leaves one half at the sluice and carries the other to the next person on duty. The next guard checks whether the two pieces fit, making the rota accountable without a written register.
Rules also extend beyond the village boundary. Under a customary agreement known as the bandabas, Phey’s share of stream water from Phyang is protected from late evening until early morning during periods of scarcity after 21 June. It is one example of the traditional water systems of India that combine infrastructure with community rules.
Who watches the cattle?
Water is not the only resource that needs protecting. During the growing season, livestock straying into cultivated fields can destroy crops. Across Ladakh, the lorapa traditionally monitors free-grazing animals and prevents them from entering fields. Research documents this role as a regional institution; it does not establish that every village, including Phey today, follows it unchanged.
An animal found grazing where it should not can be taken to a lora, an enclosed cattle pound or cattle jail. Its owner must pay the penalty set under community rules to get it back. This makes each household responsible for protecting a neighbour’s crops.
The lorapa is generally selected for the cropping season, with duties and penalties agreed by the community. The goba, or village head, oversees village affairs, resolves disputes and coordinates these roles. Together, they form a local system of checks and responsibilities rather than one office doing everything.
A system under pressure
These arrangements developed in a landscape where farming depends on short growing seasons, limited cultivable land, and water from snow and ice. The region’s wider water crisis makes fair access all the more consequential. Ladakh’s ice stupas and community-built artificial glaciers are other examples of adapting water storage and distribution to these constraints.
But customary governance is not frozen in time. Research published in 2023 and 2025 describes pressures on Ladakh’s agropastoral systems, including tourism, new livelihoods, changing livestock patterns, fencing, and the overlap between traditional institutions and formal Panchayati Raj structures. The goba’s authority has weakened in some places, while fewer people may be available for seasonal duties such as the lorapa’s.
It depends on people continuing to participate, accepting shared rules and trusting others to do their turn. In Phey, even the stone-checking method shows how cooperation is reinforced by practical ways to discourage shortcuts.
A government outreach camp in Phey in November 2025 also recorded residents raising concerns about water scarcity, roads, school facilities and connectivity. Traditional institutions do not replace public services or remove the need for investment. They show how a village can organise the resources and responsibilities closest to home.
At this altitude, the rota is more than a timetable: shared resources depend on people keeping their word.

title: Uttarakhand Forest Fires: How Women Are Leading Community Forest Protection
description: Women in Uttarakhand are leading community forest restoration and fire prevention as migration reshapes Himalayan villages. Discover how initiatives in Manar and other villages are protecting forests and livelihoods.
author: Sriroopa Dutta
content:
Every morning, 75-year-old Bhagirathi Devi walks into the forest beside her village in Uttarakhand's Champawat district. She patrols the area, returns home around noon and heads back for another round at 2 pm, often staying until sunset.
Her task is to ensure that nobody cuts trees, damages vegetation or allows cattle to graze where they should not.
For more than two decades, Bhagirathi has helped protect and restore this forest in Manar village. Known locally as Van Amma, she began the effort in 2000, when the woodland had become almost barren following years of excessive grazing and tree felling.
Today, the community-managed forest is also a site of fire prevention.
In a report published by Down To Earth on 31 May 2025, journalist Bhagirath documented how the village's women organised themselves to restore the forest, regulate access, and remove dry leaves and pine needles before the fire season.
According to residents, there has been no forest fire in the restored forest since the initiative began. The Champawat Forest Department has also recognised the effort as a model for fire prevention.
Manar's experience points to something important about forest protection in Uttarakhand: preventing fires is not always about reaching a burning hillside with firefighting equipment. It can begin much earlier, with people who understand the forest, depend on it and have the authority to regulate how it is used.
Across the state's mountain villages, women are increasingly taking on this responsibility.
As men migrate in search of employment, women remain to manage agriculture, livestock and household needs. Their daily work brings them into close contact with forests, making them among the first to notice smoke and respond to small fires.
The Ghost Village question: who is left to protect the forest?
Uttarakhand's migration story is often told through the image of the ghost village: a settlement where houses remain locked, agricultural fields lie fallow, and only a handful of residents remain.
The scale of depopulation is reflected in government figures cited in the 2021 report Locked Houses, Fallow Lands: Climate Change and Migration in Uttarakhand, India, prepared by The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) and the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research.
According to the 2011 Census, 1,048 of Uttarakhand's 16,793 revenue villages were uninhabited. A subsequent survey by the state's Rural Development and Migration Commission in 2018 identified another 734 villages that had become uninhabited after 2011.
The report notes that depopulation has affected all 13 districts, although the problem is more pronounced in the hill districts.
However, not every village affected by migration is entirely deserted. In many settlements, men have moved to towns and cities for work while women, children and older residents remain. Women continue cultivating fields, looking after cattle, collecting forest produce and caring for family members.
This changes who is available to respond when a forest fire breaks out.
In Manar, Bhagirathi Devi's initiative began with a problem familiar to many women in mountain villages. Before the forest was restored, women had to walk seven to eight kilometres to a neighbouring forest, Siddhmandir, to collect fodder and firewood. Bhagirathi told Down To Earth that this journey took five to six hours every day.
The loss of nearby forest cover had also affected the flow of local springs. Restoring the woodland was therefore not simply a conservation exercise. It was an attempt to make village life more sustainable.
For women who remain, the responsibility is consequently twofold: maintaining households in villages with fewer working-age residents and protecting the natural resources that make those settlements habitable.
Why women are often the first to notice a fire
The reasons women become first responders are closely connected to the division of labour in rural households.
Collecting firewood and fodder, taking cattle to graze, gathering leaves and working on agricultural land are routine responsibilities for many women in Uttarakhand. These activities keep them in and around forests for several hours a day.
When a fire begins, they may notice the first signs of smoke before it becomes visible from the village or reaches the attention of forest officials.
A 2023 paper by researchers Ripu Daman Singh, Surabhi Gumber, R C Sundriyal, Jeet Ram and Surendra P Singh, published in Tropical Ecology, provides important context for understanding this relationship.
Titled Chir pine forest and pre-monsoon drought determine spatial and temporal patterns of forest fires in Uttarakhand Himalaya, the research analysed satellite-derived fire data from 2002 to 2020 across 24 forest divisions in the state.
The researchers recorded 80,440 fire detections over the 19 years. Their analysis found that warmer pre-monsoon temperatures, a greater proportion of chir pine forest and lower winter and pre-monsoon rainfall together explained 56% of the variation in fire incidence.
They also noted that human activities associated with farming and the collection of fuel and fodder influence the likelihood of fires.
The paper specifically recommends examining changes in population distribution and communities' dependence on forests as part of effective fire management.
This is where women's everyday relationship with forests becomes relevant.
They are not simply residents living near a fire-prone landscape. Their livelihoods are directly connected to the condition of that landscape.
A fire can mean losing fodder for cattle, travelling farther to collect fuelwood, spending additional hours searching for forest produce and, in some cases, losing agricultural resources.
The relationship between gender and firefighting is not simply a question of who is more willing to respond. It is also a question of who is expected to undertake the work when the forest that sustains the household is threatened.
In a report published by Mongabay on 8 September 2026, journalist Swati Thapa documented this pattern in Uttarakhand villages.
Researcher Kavya Pandey of the Centre for Wildlife Studies, Bengaluru, told Thapa that traditional gender roles and women's responsibility for household work and caregiving help explain why they are often the first to respond to fires.
This offers a field-level account of a wider connection between women's labour and forest protection.
How a community can stop a fire before it spreads
Manar offers a particularly useful example of what happens when women move beyond responding to individual fires and take responsibility for managing an entire forest.
When Bhagirathi Devi began the initiative in 2000, she brought other women together to form a van panchayat, a community forest-management council. She was unanimously elected its first sarpanch.
The initial work involved clearing and fencing parts of the degraded forest. The women also worked with BAIF Development Research Foundation, a Pune-based organisation involved in silvopasture initiatives in the region.
Silvopasture combines trees, grasses and livestock management. The idea was to restore vegetation while ensuring that the community could continue to access fodder and other forest resources.
With BAIF's support and training, residents fenced the woodland using stones and thorny plants. They cleared invasive species such as lantana and planted native trees and fodder species, including banj oak (Quercus leucotrichophora), angu (Fraxinus micrantha) and utish (Alnus nepalensis).
For two years, grazing was prohibited to allow the vegetation to recover. It took another five to six years for the trees to establish themselves.
According to Manju Manral, the first president of Manar's Silvopasture Management Committee, 11.6 hectares of forest were eventually revived.
The work was not entirely voluntary.
Down To Earth reported that women involved in the restoration received Rs 120 per day from BAIF. They voluntarily contributed 10% of their wages towards maintaining the forest. Each household also contributed Rs 20 a month towards Bhagirathi's salary for guarding the woodland.
A separate 2022 field study by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, BAIF and the Centre for Ecology Development and Research also found that the forest under Manar's van panchayat was healthier than the forest outside its management area.
What the 2026 fire season reveals
In an assessment published on 2 June 2026 on the Indian Institute of Remote Sensing's (IIRS) Sudoor Manthan science portal, researchers Athira V Mukundan, Madhusmita Murmu, Chandra Mohan Bhatt and Arijit Roy analysed forest-fire activity across the state between January and May 2026.
Using NASA's MODIS active-fire data, they recorded:
- January: 200 active-fire detections.
- February: 113 detections.
- March: 178 detections.
- April: 207 detections.
- May: 433 detections.
The May figure represented a 109% increase over April. It also accounted for approximately 38% of all detections recorded between January and May.
Pauri Garhwal recorded the highest cumulative number of detections during the five-month period, at 207, followed by Chamoli with 190 and Tehri Garhwal with 130.
The researchers also used Sentinel-2 satellite imagery to map burned areas in Pauri Garhwal. Comparing images from April with those captured between 25 and 28 May, they identified approximately 838.66 sq km of burned area. Most of this was classified as low-severity burning, while 0.94 sq km fell into the highest severity category.
These figures are satellite-based detections and mapped burn areas, not a count of independently verified individual fires. Nevertheless, they show how quickly fire activity intensified towards the end of the pre-monsoon season.
The 2023 research by Singh and his colleagues helps explain this seasonal pattern.
Most fires in Uttarakhand occur between March and May, when temperatures rise, vegetation dries and fresh pine litter accumulates on the forest floor.
The human cost of these fires can be severe. On 13 June 2024, four forest department personnel died while fighting a blaze in Binsar Wildlife Sanctuary in Almora district. According to a report by The Times of India on 14 June 2024, four others were seriously injured after the firefighting team was engulfed by flames.
For women who fight smaller fires in community forests, the risks are no less real, particularly when they have no protective clothing, footwear or firefighting equipment.
Besides, women's participation does not automatically translate into decision-making power.
A 2026 research chapter by K Nagahama, published in Springer Proceedings in Earth and Environmental Sciences, examines women's participation in a Uttarakhand van panchayat through household surveys, interviews, forest surveys and long-term observations conducted between 2011 and 2023.
The research examines an important distinction: being present in community forest management does not necessarily mean having equal authority over decisions or control over resources.
The problem is also visible in the reporting from Uttarakhand.
In her September 2026 Mongabay investigation, Swati Thapa spoke to Laxmi Kharayat, a field trainer with The Hunger Project, who described cases where women formally listed as van panchayat heads were unaware of their positions, while male family members exercised authority on their behalf.
There is also a gap between the work women undertake and the employment opportunities available to them.
Seasonal fire watchers recruited by the forest department are predominantly men. Women who assist in firefighting often do so without regular wages or access to appropriate protective equipment.
The Forest Fire Prevention and Management Scheme and India's National Action Plan on Forest Fires recognise the importance of early detection, community participation and coordinated firefighting. The challenge is to ensure that these provisions translate into practical support for women at the village level.
This means providing women with training in fire prevention and safe firefighting, protective clothing, gloves, sturdy footwear, communication equipment and access to emergency assistance.
It also means creating paid opportunities for women as seasonal fire watchers and ensuring that they have actual decision-making authority within van panchayats.
Just as importantly, their work should not be treated as an unpaid extension of household responsibilities simply because they are the people who remain in the village.
Forest protection begins with the people who depend on it
Bhagirathi Devi's work did not begin with a firefighting operation. It began with a forest that had become too degraded to support the people living beside it.
By bringing women together, restoring native vegetation, regulating grazing and establishing a system for removing dry litter, the village created a model of long-term community protection.
For women in Uttarakhand's mountain villages, protecting a forest also means protecting the resources that keep their households functioning.
When the forest burns, the consequences reach their cattle, farms, water sources and daily routines. Their leadership has shown that communities can play a significant role in preventing fires, provided they have the authority and resources to do so.
The next step is to ensure that this responsibility does not remain invisible or unpaid.
The women who recognise the first signs of smoke, organise their neighbours and maintain village forests should be treated as essential partners in forest protection, not as an informal firefighting force expected to manage with whatever tools they have at hand.

title: Watching a Press Wallah Discard Charcoal Inspired This Schoolgirl to Design a Solar Ironing Cart
description: For generations, India's neighbourhood press wallahs have relied on burning charcoal to earn a living. Watching one of them dispose of burnt charcoal prompted Tamil Nadu schoolgirl Vinisha Umashankar to explore an alternative.
author: Vaishali Gautam
content:
From school uniforms to office shirts, many of us rely on our neighbourhood press wallahs for freshly ironed clothes. The history of the tool they use goes back over 2,000 years, long before electricity entered our homes.
As early as the first century BC, people in China used metal pans filled with hot charcoal to remove creases from fabric. These heated pans were moved over stretched cloth to smooth out wrinkles.
In medieval Europe, blacksmiths made heavy, flat metal irons known as sadirons. These were heated over a fire or on a stove. Since they cooled down during use, people often kept several irons ready to use in rotation.
Charcoal irons offered another way to keep the metal base hot. Their hollow bodies held burning charcoal. In 1852, a patent was granted for a design featuring a chimney and ventilation openings.
In India, generations of dhobis, istriwallas and neighbourhood press wallahs have earned their livelihoods through washing and ironing clothes. Their work requires an understanding of different fabrics, heat and pressure.
The history of India's laundry trade is also linked to caste and hereditary occupations. For many families belonging to traditional washer communities, the skills involved in washing and ironing clothes have been passed down through generations.
In 1882, American inventor Henry W Seely patented an electric flat iron. His design used electricity to generate heat, eliminating the need to heat the iron over a fire or burn charcoal inside it.
Despite advances in ironing technology, charcoal irons remain a familiar sight on Indian streets. However, burning charcoal exposes vendors to smoke and contributes to air pollution. Producing charcoal can also contribute to deforestation.
At the age of 12, Vinisha Umashankar from Tiruvannamalai, Tamil Nadu, noticed an ironing vendor discarding burnt charcoal on her way home from school. She began researching its environmental impact and looking for a cleaner alternative.
Vinisha designed a mobile ironing cart that uses solar panels and batteries to power a steam iron. The cart could also accommodate mobile phone charging facilities, giving vendors another potential source of income.
The National Innovation Foundation developed a prototype in 2019. Two years later, Vinisha became the youngest finalist for the inaugural Earthshot Prize and, at 15, addressed world leaders at COP26 in Glasgow.
For centuries, people have found different ways to heat irons and remove creases from clothes. Vinisha's invention explores how an everyday service that supports generations of Indian families could become less dependent on charcoal.

title: Nvidia Reinstates Huang as AI Industry Faces Leadership Risks
description: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after a boardroom reversal backed by Donald Trump, sending shares soaring and raising questions about corporate power.
author: Frontline News Desk
content:
Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as president and chief executive officer of the world’s chipmaker by market value, marking a reversal in the history of the company and driving the stock to its biggest rally in decades. Fewer than two weeks after Huang departed Nvidia under the shadow of scandal, he is reclaiming both titles, the board stated in an announcement on November 23. US President Donald Trump had lobbied for the reinstatement, and the board cited input from the government of the United States when issuing the statement.
“Thank you all for the second chance. I am going to be a better CEO the second time around,” Huang told employees at Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California. Chairman Harvey C. Jones said in the statement, "The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.”
Huang’s return follows weeks of turmoil at Nvidia, whose technology underpins the boom in artificial intelligence. The board had ousted him earlier this month after revelations that he had engaged in affairs outside his marriage—one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom the government of the US has investigated for espionage on behalf of China.
Supporters both within and outside the company, however, regarded the 63-year-old executive as irreplaceable. Huang had transformed Nvidia from a supplier of graphics chips into an enterprise valued at more than $5 trillion, while travelling the globe to champion AI as a revolution in industry.
News of his reinstatement sparked a rally for Nvidia. Shares surged 31 per cent to $165.05 in New York, marking the company’s highest gain in a single day since May 2003. Prior to the rebound, the stock had declined by roughly a third over the course of the year, erasing about $1.5 trillion in value on the market.
Nvidia’s board stated that its investigation into reports concerning Huang will continue, while the executive faces scrutiny from Congress over both his conduct and the export of technology to China. Huang is scheduled to sit for an interview with three committees of the House on December 1 and to testify before the Senate Banking Committee two days later at a hearing on export controls of the US. The company is still under scrutiny from investigators, including at the FBI and on Capitol Hill.
No consultation
People familiar with the deliberations said the board acted without consulting interim CEO Colette Kress or other executives, following an intervention by Trump, who pressed directors to make the move. Huang had appealed to the board for his return—a bid backed by some employees and prominent figures in Silicon Valley—after directors initially rejected his overture. The reversal echoed events at OpenAI in 2023, when Sam Altman was ousted as CEO and reinstated within a week amid backlash from investors and staff; like Huang, Altman is regarded as central to the development of AI.
Huang ranks as Nvidia’s fifth-largest shareholder with a stake of roughly 3.6 per cent, though he holds no shares with voting privileges of the kind that grant founders such as Mark Zuckerberg of Meta Platforms and Elon Musk of SpaceX control over their companies.
The executive relies on a style of management that involves intervening in problems at Nvidia and overseeing roughly 60 reports, nearly all in roles within engineering, including specialists in memory chips, networking, and graphics and processors.
“A lot of companies’ organisation charts, they all look the same. And it doesn’t make any sense to me. The architecture of the ‌company should reflect the environment in which it exists,” Huang said on a podcast in March. Huang has involved himself in the operations of startups backed by Nvidia, assisting them in securing customers and joining fundraising calls to attract investors, according to founders, venture capitalists, and a former Nvidia employee.
Huang’s return stumped many, and US lawmakers from both the Democratic and Republican parties strongly objected to his reinstatement. But it also reinforced the idea that some tech CEOs were considered irreplaceable, a big risk for ‌a company critical to the AI industry.
Speaking at a press conference in Brooklyn on November 23, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said: “I do not think that working people across the country signed up for their pensions being tied to the question of Jensen Huang’s fidelity to his marriage, and yet, for many days, that had a massive impact.”
He added, “We’re speaking about a divorce settlement that has been rumoured to be around $81 billion. That would be the cost of providing universal child care for every 3- and 4-year-old in the United States of America for an entire year. And a lot of this just brings to mind what Justice Brandeis said quite some time ago, which is, "We can have democracy; we can have great wealth concentrated in the hands of a few; we cannot have both.”
Nvidia leads the market in manufacturing accelerators for artificial intelligence—the chips used to train and run AI models—making the company a beneficiary of spending on infrastructure for data centres. The US government restricts sales of these chips to China, and Nvidia’s ties to the country, alongside its compliance with export controls, have drawn scrutiny.
Late last year, following lobbying from Huang, Trump loosened controls on chips and permitted Nvidia to sell its H200 processor—now generations behind its Vera Rubin line—to China. Last week, Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, informed investors that the chipmaker would halt sales of licensed H200 products to the country.
The company will hire a new chief compliance officer, and the board recently formed a committee to oversee national security and export control matters, it said in a statement.
Tech firms soar
News of Huang’s return, released shortly after the opening bell on November 23, sparked a surge across equities, driving shares of Nvidia up by 31.5 per cent and adding more than $900 billion to the valuation of the company. Other firms on Wall Street also drew buying interest, lifting the Nasdaq by more than six per cent, the S&P 500 by 4.7 per cent, and the Dow by three percent.
Markets in Asia, which had opened the week with losses, followed that trajectory. Taipei led the region with a nine per cent gain as chipmakers TSMC and MediaTek each rose nearly 10 per cent. Seoul climbed more than six per cent on advances from SK Hynix and Samsung.
Tokyo closed nearly four per cent higher, propelled by jumps of 12.5 per cent in Advantest, 7.7 per cent in Tokyo Electron, and 10 per cent in Kioxia. Exchanges in Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington, Bangkok, and Manila also posted gains, while Hong Kong slipped as technology firms in China lagged behind the rally.
China’s warning
Huang’s comeback—prompted by the intervention of Trump—drew caution from state media in China. Less than three hours after the board issued its announcement, the Global Times published a commentary urging China to “remain vigilant”.
The article said, “It is foreseeable that the malicious attempts to sow discord in China-US relations will not automatically disappear simply because Huang has been reinstated.” It added that the next round of “witch hunts” could include investigation letters, delays in export licences and congressional hearings.
